$comment: CLAIMS WE ONCE PUBLISHED THAT ARE NO LONGER TRUE.
WHY THIS FILE EXISTS. On 31 Aug 2026 four factual errors were found in
woocommerce-too-slow. Three of them were about vendor behaviour that had
changed. The uncomfortable part: spec-facts.json ALREADY carried the correct
cart-fragments fact, verified 25 Aug, citing the same WooCommerce developer
post used to confirm it. The research had been done. The prose had never been
reconciled with it, and nothing in the build noticed the contradiction.
spec_freshness.py guards the DATA going stale. Nothing guarded the PROSE
drifting away from the data. This file closes that gap.
WHAT IT IS NOT. It cannot detect a claim nobody has found yet. It is a
regression test, not a fact-checker: once a wrong claim has been identified
and removed, this stops it coming back in a rewrite, a merge, or a new post
by an author who learned the old behaviour and never heard it changed. That
is the actual failure mode here, so that is what it defends against.
ADDING AN ENTRY. Whenever you correct a factual claim about a third party,
record the SUPERSEDED assertion here, not the corrected one. Point
supersededBy at the spec-facts key that now holds the truth, if one exists.
WRITING THE PATTERN. Match the assertion, not the topic. Too broad and the
guard fires on the corrected text and gets switched off, which is worse than
not having it. Run the guard immediately after adding an entry: it must pass
against the corrected page. Two escape hatches exist for that:
historicalOk  - a match is allowed when the prose is describing the old
behaviour as history ('used to', 'before 7.8', 'changed in')
requiresNearby- a match is allowed when the page also carries the current
fact somewhere, which is how you permit a fuller
explanation without permitting the bare old claim

claims.retiredAssertion: The cart-fragments script is enqueued on every page of a WooCommerce store.
claims.whatChanged: WooCommerce 7.8 (June 2023) stopped enqueueing it on all page routes. It now loads only where the Cart Widget renders, where third-party code declares wc-cart-fragments as a dependency, or where it is explicitly enqueued. Many themes hardcode the widget, so it still happens often, but it is no longer the default.

claims.retiredAssertion: wc-ajax=get_refreshed_fragments is the request you see when a shopper adds to cart.
claims.whatChanged: The add itself is wc-ajax=add_to_cart on a classic store, or a POST to /wc/store/v1/cart/add-item on a block store. get_refreshed_fragments is the separate follow-up call that redraws the mini-cart. Naming only the second one describes the wrong request.

claims.retiredAssertion: Every checkout page load contacts the payment provider and writes the order.
claims.whatChanged: Neither happens on page load. The initial load builds the form and totals; changing an address or shipping method fires an AJAX recalculation; the payment provider is contacted and the order written only after the shopper presses Place Order. Conflating the three misdirects anyone optimising a slow checkout.

claims.retiredAssertion: WooCommerce does not build responsive image sets.
claims.whatChanged: WordPress core has emitted srcset and sizes markup since version 4.4, so responsive candidates exist on any WooCommerce store. What is genuinely missing is WebP/AVIF conversion and an upload size cap. Saying there are no image sets sends readers after the wrong fix.

claims.retiredAssertion: The MyCustomPatches project cut hosting from $150/month to $0/month.
claims.whatChanged: Retired, not pending: no hosting invoices were kept and the client does not recall the amount, so nothing can be reconciled and no figure can honestly be restored. See the hosting-cost metric in case-study-facts.json, which carries permanent: true for the same reason. Registered 15 Sep 2026 after the French and German dictionaries were found still publishing the figure in a directory this guard did not scan. SCOPE, corrected the same day: an earlier version of this entry also retired the ranking claim and said no dated confirmation is held. The delivery time, 13 templates and zero downtime remained in the approved project record. The earlier 200+ URL count was withdrawn after an owner correction on 3 Oct 2026; no replacement count is published. Rankings are recorded as none lost in the 30 days after launch from a Search Console monitoring window.

claims.retiredAssertion: PandaCodeGen's Scale tier costs $5,000 to $10,000, so our published tiers run from $1,500 to $10,000.
claims.whatChanged: Scale has no published ceiling. Commit 8aeefe9c (9 Sep 2026) retired the $5,000 to $10,000 range, and the canon in src/data/company-facts.ts now reads Starter from $1,500, Growth from $3,500 and Scale from $5,000, with work above that quoted after a scoping call. Twenty-four copies of the old range survived that sweep in blog FAQ answers (one of them in FAQPage structured data), cost guides and a case study, because the range was often split across a line break or written as $5K to $10K or as a $1,500 to $10,000 span of our tiers. Registered 4 Oct 2026 when those were fixed. The pattern only fires when the range is tied to Scale or to our own tiers, so market figures such as an agency's $10,000+ minimum stay allowed.

claims.retiredAssertion: Included post-launch support is 15 business days for Starter and 30 business days for Growth and Scale.
claims.whatChanged: Owner-confirmed 9 Oct 2026: support is counted in calendar days (15 for Starter, 30 for Growth, Scale and upgraded projects) and starts on the day the site goes live. The canon is POST_LAUNCH_SUPPORT in src/data/company-facts.ts. Registered 10 Oct 2026 after an independent review found the old business-day wording still on two tier cards in /blog/cheap-web-developer. The pattern only fires on 15 or 30 business days tied to support, so reply times (one business day) and refund settlement (10 to 12 business days) stay allowed.
